en: The Svargaparva (The Book of Heaven)
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jaya). Bhmj 18.1.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira beheld the Kuru king, who resembled Śakra, adorned with the splendor of heaven, radiant with a crown and armlets.
Seeing Śatakratu there with his younger brother, he became filled with indignation and said:
"May it be well with the gods; here is my salutation with joined palms to heaven."
There, upon a supreme throne as formidable as a peak of Mount Sumeru, sat the wicked Duryodhana, the cause of the earth’s destruction.
I have no dwelling there; I am departing now—homage be to you!
Where my heroic brothers are, there is my dwelling now.
While the king was speaking thus, the gods then said to the divine messenger, who was as swift as thought: "Go now toward his brothers."
Proceeding immediately along the path pointed out by the divine messenger,
he beheld terrifying men dwelling within the depths of hell.
In that place, slippery with a mass of hair, blood, flesh, gore, and fat, drenched and strewn with many corpses, and teeming with worms; (Bhājana-loka 18.8)
Surrounded on all sides by faces like those of crows, herons, cranes, and owls,
it was crowded with hundreds of dense collisions, thick with the foul stench of corpses.
On the banks of sands heated by saws, stones,
and boiling oil, and amidst the horrors of jars of blood and fat, and the thorny *śalmali* trees, [the hell-beings suffer].
In that place terrifying with razors, thorns, spikes, and blazing pillars,
its sands were filled with the foul-smelling pus of the heated Vaitaraṇī river.
There, in that place dense with terrible darkness and filled with the cries of men and women being sliced by the sword-leaf forest, the son of Dharma heard [the following].
O King, do not turn back from here for even a single moment with these cool [winds], while the cries of the sinners being boiled—so harsh to the heart—are heard. (Bhājana-vastu 18.13)
Touched by the breezes of your merit, the darkness afflicts us;
we are your brothers, the Pāṇḍavas, headed by Bhīma.
And this Kṛṣṇā, the beautiful-waisted, beloved, and virtuous queen—
having heard this piteous news, the king was as if split apart by a thunderbolt.
Remaining right there, free from the pairs of opposites and censuring the capriciousness of fate, he said:
"Alas! The intellect of the gods is surely destroyed by a lack of reflection."
Those by whom these people, devoted to the Dharma, were neglected during this time of affliction—this is delusion; such a thing is not clarity or discernment.
Those who do not perceive the transgression of dharma among the wise, wondering, "Is this an error, a dream, or an illusion? What is this? (Bhj 18.18).
"O divine messenger, I do not know whose this wicked behavior is.
I shall remain right here; go away, for I have no need for heaven."
"Where the wicked are honored and the virtuous are indeed slaughtered"—
having been addressed thus by Dharmarāja, the divine messenger [spoke] to the Lord of the Gods.
Having gone there, he reported everything, and he [the Lord] returned in silence;
when the Lord of the Gods arrived there along with the deities headed by Dharma, [he spoke].
Nothing inauspicious was seen, and a virtuous breeze blew;
then the Lord of the Gods spoke to Viṣṇu, the delighter of Dharma.
"This is not false; it was indeed shown by me here.
This vision is for kings who perform mixed deeds. (Bhājana-vastu 18.23)
"Since even a slight touch of untruth has occurred to you through this killing of Droṇa,
come and behold your own brothers, who have attained their divine station."
When the King of the Gods had thus spoken of the splendor of heaven, Pāñcālī, and his sons who had attained immortality, Yudhiṣṭhira was freed from his grief.
Having bathed in the celestial Ganges water, which shone like the sky, with the voice of Dharma,
he cast off his human state and went to the holy assembly of the gods.
There he beheld his own younger brothers, who had ascended to their own station, along with the Gandharvas and Kinnaras whose limbs were graced by the dances of the Apsarases.
And in the solar mandala, Karṇa was personally shown by Indra,
as well as Abhimanyu, who surpassed the God of Love with his radiant form.
He is the one named Varcas, the Soma within the lunar orb;
he is the Gandharva king Dhṛtarāṣṭra himself, the lord of men.
Vasu, Śāntanava Bhīṣma, the preceptor Droṇa, Bṛhaspati,
and Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Universe, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.

Having seen those who were born on earth as portions of him and observing those who took refuge in him, the son of Dharma— a treasure of splendor— reached that state worthy of Hariścandra, which is eternally blissful and venerated by the inhabitants of Nandana.
Then, that moon among kings, whose conduct was pure, shone resplendently while being saluted on all sides by the monarchs Nahuṣa, Dilīpa, Dhundhumāra, Sagara, Bhagīratha, Rāma, and Kārtavīrya.
Having heard this narrative of the Bharatas as proclaimed by Vaiśampāyana,
Janamejaya, having completed his snake sacrifice, attained peace of mind.
Having heard this which was told by Sūta to the residents of the Naimiṣa forest, those headed by Śaunaka remained filled with overflowing joy.
Thus ends the Svargaparvan in the Bhāratamañjarī composed by Śrī Kṣemendra.
